EXTRA CLASS · HOME AND DAILY LIFE

The words of our house.

A house is a child’s first country, and this class is its phrasebook: forty-one cards walk the whole home in tour order — rooms, routines, kitchen, chores, the door, the sounds, the green habits — and every word is standing somewhere within reach of you right now. Every tile below opens its own step-by-step lesson.

HOW THIS CLASS WORKS

A house is a child’s first country. This is its phrasebook.

The Home and Daily Life class is a bonus class, kept beside the main learning path like the Toddler Room and the Kitchen: the regular classes stay the core sequence, and this one is for families with a curious house-mouse in residence — the child who wants to know what the broom is for, where the mail sleeps, and what the tap is called when it runs. Forty-one cards walk the whole home, and your actual house is the classroom: every word on every card is standing somewhere within reach of you right now.

The cards run in tour order on purpose. The rooms come first, because rooms hold everything else; then the routines that open and close the day; then the kitchen, the chores and the tools; then the edges of home — the door, the mail, the pets — and the sounds the house makes when nobody is watching; and the last group is the quiet one: the safety words and the green habits that keep a home kind.

THE CLASS GAME

The house hunt.

Call a word from the cards — "sink!" "cushion!" "doormat!" — and your child runs to touch the real thing. That is the whole game, and it never gets old, because your home is the answer key: every word is findable, every find is a sprint, and every sprint burns the word in deep. Play it room by room, or whole-house championship rules; the vacuum cleaner card is always requested first.

SAME HOME, TWO WORDS

Tap and faucet. Torch and flashlight. Both are right.

English grew up on several shores, and this class says so out loud. The cards carry the everyday words of the US, UK and Canada — and where the countries differ, both words ride along in the teaching: the tap and the faucet, the torch and the flashlight, the wardrobe and the closet, the trolley and the shopping cart, the bin and the trash can, the parcel and the package, the garden and the yard. Whichever your family says, your child hears both — and learns early that words, like homes, come in kinds.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Rooms at Home — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the five rooms as a tour of your real home: the card is the map, and the house is the territory.

What is this?

A home is divided into rooms, and each room has a name that says what happens there: sleeping, cooking, washing, gathering, growing.

What does it mean?

Room names are the first map words a child owns. Once the five are known, every instruction you give — take this to the kitchen — becomes followable, and every question your child asks becomes askable.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and a house — any house. The tour takes five minutes and ends with your child standing in the right room when you call it out.

Why this matters

Children learn location words fastest when their legs carry them there. A card on the couch cannot do what a sprint to the bathroom does.

What it teaches

Spatial vocabulary (in, where, which room), category thinking (a house is rooms; a room is things), and the confidence of navigating home territory by name.

Words to learn

bedroomkitchenbathroomliving roomgardenroomhouse

Say this to your child

“"Rooms at home — let us take the tour! Where do we sleep? Run there! Where does the food cook? Go! You know every room in this house."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "five rooms, one house — let us find them all."
  2. Tour the real house in the card order: bedroom, kitchen, bathroom, living room, then out the door to the garden or yard.
  3. In each room, one anchor sentence: "this is where we sleep" — and one object: point to the bed.
  4. Back on the couch, cover the card and ask "which room has the sofa?"
  5. Finish standing in the room your child loves best — the game ends with a win.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Rooms at Home" sit over five small scenes side by side: a bed in the bedroom, a stove in the kitchen, a sink and shower in the bathroom, a sofa in the living room, and a fenced garden with a tree.

Ask your child

"Which room do we cook in?" "Which room has your bed?" "Where does the soap live?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might announce room names at random all day — "bathroom!" — drag the card on the tour like a treasure map, or ask where the rooms are in grandma’s house.

Out in the real world

Every home you visit — a friend’s flat, a hotel, a holiday cottage — has the same five rooms wearing the same names. The words pack themselves for every trip.

Try it together

Room Race: call a room, the child runs to it, touches one true thing in it and runs back for the next call. Three rounds and the map is permanent. Grown-up runs the last round — and loses dramatically.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many rooms on the card?" (five) "Where do we sleep?" (the bedroom) "What do we call the outside room?" (the garden — or the yard)

This lesson pairs with the Rooms at Home flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Parts of the Home (Inside) — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the fixed parts of a home by touch: the child finds each part in your real house, and the words attach to the touching.

What is this?

Inside every home are the parts that do not move: windows that let light in, doors that open, stairs that climb, walls that hold, floors that carry.

What does it mean?

These five words are the skeleton of every direction and every safety rule a child will hear at home — feet on the floor, hand on the rail, close the door. Owning the words makes the rules sayable.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and one hallway. The touch-hunt needs no props: a window, a door, a wall and a floor are always within reach, and the stairs are wherever they are.

Why this matters

A child who can name the parts can also ask about them — "why is the wall cold?" — and every question about a fixed part is a question about how a home works.

What it teaches

Vocabulary for fixed structures, body-safe navigation (stairs with a hand), and the first glimmer that a house is a made thing, built of parts that were chosen.

Words to learn

windowdoorstairswallfloorinsidepart

Say this to your child

“"Parts of the home — touch hunt! Hand on the wall, feet on the floor, one door, one window. The stairs are the slowest part — we take them with a hand."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and read the five words slowly, touching each picture.
  2. Stand in the hallway: "find a wall" — hand on it. "Find the floor" — feet on it.
  3. Find a door and open-close it once, gently. Find a window and look through it.
  4. At the stairs: hand on the rail, feet on the floor, slow climb, counting steps aloud.
  5. Back at the card, ask your child to point to the part they touched first.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Parts of the Home" sit over five inside pieces: a blue-framed window, a closed door, a staircase with a rail, a plain wall and a wide floor.

Ask your child

"What does the window do?" (lets light in) "What do we hold at the stairs?" (the rail — our hand on it) "What is under your feet right now?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might pat every wall in the house like a drum, announce FLOOR at each room change, or ask why the window cannot open all the way.

Out in the real world

Offices, libraries and grandparent homes all have the same five parts. The touch-hunt replays itself everywhere you go — and stairs in new places get the careful version automatically.

Try it together

Parts Bingo: draw a tiny five-square grid on paper — window, door, stairs, wall, floor. Walk the house and mark each square as the child finds and touches the real part. Full card, full pride.

Staying safe

Stairs come with their rule attached, said the same way every time: hand on the rail, feet on the floor, one step at a time. The rule and the word grow up together.

This lesson pairs with the Parts of the Home (Inside) flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Parts of a Home (Outside) — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the outside of a home as a reading exercise: the house is the book, and the curb is the reading chair.

What is this?

From the outside a home shows the parts that face the world: the front door, the windows, the roof on top, the chimney that used to carry smoke, the garage that shelters the car.

What does it mean?

Outside parts are how children learn that homes come in kinds — with garages and without, flat roofs and pointy. "Some homes do, some don’t" is the sentence this lesson plants.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and a window or doorstep with a view of any house. No walking required for round one; the street does the showing.

Why this matters

House-watching is calm, free and endlessly available. A child who can read a house’s parts from a distance has a five-minute game that works in every neighborhood on Earth.

What it teaches

Observation from distance, comparison (this roof, that roof), and honest variation — the same word can fit different-looking homes.

Words to learn

front doorroofchimneygaragewindowoutside

Say this to your child

“"Parts of a home — outside! There is our front door, there is the roof sitting on top like a hat. Does our house have a chimney? Let us look!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "every part on this card is outside — let us spot them."
  2. From the window or step, find your own front door, then your roof.
  3. Hunt for a chimney (some houses have none — say so) and a garage.
  4. Count the windows you can see from where you stand.
  5. Next walk, repeat from the curb — a different house each time.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Parts of a Home" sit over a pale-blue front door, a four-pane window, a blue-tiled roof, a brick chimney and a garage with its door down.

Ask your child

"What is on top of the house?" (the roof) "Where does the car sleep?" (the garage — if there is one) "Which part do guests knock on?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might declare every roof a hat, ask why some chimneys are quiet, or point out garages for the whole length of the street.

Out in the real world

House-reading travels: on any drive, any walk, any storybook picture, the five outside parts are findable. Buildings in books get read with the same words.

Try it together

House I-Spy: "I spy with my little eye a part of a home that is red" — the roof, the door, whatever fits. Five finds wins; the winner picks the next house to read.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the roof do?" (sits on top, keeps the rain out) "Where does smoke come from when there is a fire?" (the chimney) "What part do we knock?" (the front door)

This lesson pairs with the Parts of a Home (Outside) flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Living Room Words — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the living room without anyone standing up: the sofa is the classroom, and everything taught is within pointing distance.

What is this?

The living room is the gathering room: the sofa to sit on, the television to watch, the coffee table to rest a cup, the floor lamp for light, the remote control for the deciding.

What does it mean?

Children already own this room — naming its parts makes their favorite territory official. Vocabulary that attaches to comfort sticks faster than vocabulary that attaches to lessons.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the sofa. Round one is five pointing answers from sitting down; round two is the swap-seats version, which refreshes the answers for free.

Why this matters

The living room is where families talk, so it is where family vocabulary pays off daily: put it on the coffee table, sit on the sofa, lamp on for reading.

What it teaches

Object naming in context, positional words (on, under, beside — where IS the remote?), and turn-taking in a seated game.

Words to learn

sofatelevisioncoffee tablefloor lampremote controlliving room

Say this to your child

“"Living room words — from the best seat in the house! Sofa under us, television there, lamp in the corner. Now — where is that remote hiding?"”

Step by step

  1. Sit on the sofa with the card: "this room has five names on it — let us find them from here."
  2. Point at each real thing: sofa (we are on it), television, coffee table, floor lamp, remote.
  3. Swap seats and name five again — the new view finds new details.
  4. Ask: "what does the remote do?" — one button press, together, then it rests.
  5. End with the lamp: switch it on for story time, and the room has a mood you made.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Living Room Words" sit over a blue sofa with cushions, a wide television, a round coffee table, a tall floor lamp and a remote control with many buttons.

Ask your child

"Where do we sit together?" (the sofa) "What rests our cups?" (the coffee table) "Who turned the lamp on just now?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might claim the remote seat as a throne, label the whole room aloud to a stuffed audience, or put the remote exactly where the card shows it.

Out in the real world

Every gathering place has a sofa-word and a screen-word — hotels, waiting rooms, grandparents. The child who names their living room names every living room.

Try it together

Remote Hunt: hide the remote (in plain sight — under the cushion, on the coffee table, beside the lamp) and give warm-and-cold clues. The finder presses one button as the prize. The room teaches itself while you play.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where are we sitting?" (the sofa) "What is the little table called?" (the coffee table) "What do we press to choose the show?" (the remote control)

This lesson pairs with the Living Room Words flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Furniture Words — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches furniture as a category word: not five separate facts, but one big idea — the big things that stay put — with five members of the club.

What is this?

Furniture is the family of big, unmoving things in a home: the armchair, the bookshelf, the rug, the cabinet and the stool all belong to it.

What does it mean?

Category words are a leap for young minds: sofa is a thing, furniture is a kind of thing. Once the leap lands, it lands everywhere — appliances, tools, clothes — and the world sorts itself.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and five real pieces — the card’s five or your home’s five. The feel-it part matters: each piece gets touched in the way that is truest to it.

Why this matters

Furniture is the gentlest category to start with: every member is big, visible and daily. Success here makes the next category word easy.

What it teaches

Category formation (member vs kind), function thinking (what is this piece FOR), and the comparison habit — how is a stool like a chair, how is it not?

Words to learn

furniturearmchairbookshelfrugcabinetstool

Say this to your child

“"Furniture is the big-word for the things that stay put. The armchair stays, the bookshelf stays — let us visit the whole family and ask each one: what is your job?"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "all five of these belong to one family called furniture."
  2. Visit the real pieces: sit in the armchair, open and shut the cabinet once, stand on the stool beside a grown-up.
  3. Kneel on the rug — "the rug is furniture you can feel with your knees."
  4. Ask the one-job question at each piece: what does the bookshelf do? What does the stool do?
  5. Count the family: how many furniture pieces in this room?

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Furniture Words" sit over a soft blue armchair, a bookshelf with books inside, a striped rug, a two-door cabinet and a three-legged stool.

Ask your child

"Which furniture holds books?" "Which furniture do we kneel on?" "What is the difference between a chair and a stool?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might extend the family eagerly — "is the bed furniture? the dresser?" — kneel on every rug in the house to check it is real furniture, or open the cabinet to greet the dishes.

Out in the real world

Waiting rooms, schools and libraries all have furniture — the category word works the moment you walk in. Bookshelf is the member your child will meet again first.

Try it together

Furniture Says: like Simon Says, but every command is a true furniture fact — furniture says sit, furniture says kneel, furniture says open, furniture says stand on the stool with a hand. Wrong moves are giggled at, not scored.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is the big word for big stay-put things?" (furniture) "Is the sofa furniture?" (yes) "What does the bookshelf carry?" (the books)

This lesson pairs with the Furniture Words flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Bedroom Words — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the bedroom as a sequence in disguise: the five words are the five moves of bedtime, and the child learns them by doing them.

What is this?

The bedroom keeps the bed, the pillow, the blanket, the wardrobe (the closet) and the bedside table — the five things between waking and sleeping.

What does it mean?

Bedtime resists being told and accepts being known. When the child can name and run the sequence — pillow, blanket, book, light — bedtime stops being something that happens to them.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the actual bedtime, which is the perfect classroom: the lesson IS the routine tonight, with each word said as each thing happens.

Why this matters

The wardrobe-closet pair rides along free: whichever your family says, the child now owns both names for the same door. Bedside table is the bonus word — it belongs to the child.

What it teaches

Sequencing (first pillow, then blanket, then light), ownership of a routine, and the possessive pride of my bed, my pillow, my table.

Words to learn

bedpillowblanketwardrobeclosetbedside table

Say this to your child

“"Bedroom words, in order: clothes in the wardrobe, pillow up, blanket down, book on the bedside table, light off. You know the whole goodnight by heart."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card at the bedroom door: "five words, and we will do every one of them tonight."
  2. Wardrobe first: open it, name the clothes hanging there — closet or wardrobe, say yours, offer both.
  3. Bed next: pillow fluffed by small hands, blanket spread by the same.
  4. Book on the bedside table — the table gets its word as the book lands.
  5. Light off with the fifth word: "bedroom words — all five. Goodnight."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Bedroom Words" sit over a made bed, a soft pillow, a folded blanket with a stripe, a tall wardrobe with two doors and a small bedside table with a drawer.

Ask your child

"Where do the clothes sleep?" (the wardrobe — the closet) "What holds your head?" "Where does the storybook live until morning?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might recite the five in bed like a countdown, insist the teddy has its own bedside spot, or teach the sequence to the wardrobe itself.

Out in the real world

Every bed away from home — hotel, grandma’s, holiday — still has a pillow, a blanket and a light. The sequence goes where the child goes, and strange bedrooms shrink to familiar words.

Try it together

Goodnight Countdown: the five words written (or drawn) on a card by the bed; the child taps each one as it happens tonight. Five taps and the card says goodnight first.

Understanding check

Ask: "What goes on first, the pillow or the blanket?" (pillow) "Where do we keep clothes?" (the wardrobe or closet) "What is the little table by the bed?" (the bedside table)

This lesson pairs with the Bedroom Words flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Bedroom Objects — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches four small objects by giving their power away: the child who opens the curtains and clicks the lamp owns the room’s light, and the words come with the ownership.

What is this?

The bedroom objects do the room’s quiet work: the lamp makes light, the curtains manage the morning, the rug warms bare feet, the alarm clock keeps the time.

What does it mean?

Objects a child controls are objects a child names. The curtain is a word twice a day — opened at wake, closed at night — and twice a day is a lot for one word.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the two reachable switches: curtains a child can pull and a lamp a child can click. The rug and the clock are pointed at, not switched.

Why this matters

The alarm clock doubles as the first clock lesson: the short hand is where we wake. Objects that do visible jobs teach their names almost by themselves.

What it teaches

Cause and effect (curtain open means morning light), time-awareness seed (the clock hands), and the responsibility glow of a real job done daily.

Words to learn

lampcurtainrugalarm clocklightmorning

Say this to your child

“"Bedroom objects! You open the curtains — hello, sun. You click the lamp — hello, story. The rug keeps your feet warm and the clock keeps the morning."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card at wake-up time: "four objects, two of them are yours."
  2. Hand over the curtains: the child opens them, and the morning arrives — "you opened the day."
  3. Point the rug: bare feet land on it, "warm, because of the rug."
  4. Introduce the alarm clock: which hand is short? Where does it point when we wake?
  5. At story time, the lamp is the child’s to click — light for reading, made by them.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Bedroom Objects" sit over a bed with a blue blanket, a lamp with a cream shade, blue curtains drawn aside, a striped rug and an alarm clock with bells on top.

Ask your child

"What makes the little pool of light at story time?" (the lamp) "What opens the morning?" (the curtains) "What says good morning before we do?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might take curtain duty so seriously it becomes the household clock, set the alarm with a grown-up for practice, or click the lamp like a lighthouse keeper.

Out in the real world

Lamps and curtains run every room in every home — the living room lamp, the kitchen curtains. The child who runs the bedroom switches starts running them everywhere.

Try it together

Light and Morning: a two-word game — the child performs "curtain" (open wide, arms out) and "lamp" (one slow click, one blink) with their whole body. Call them fast, call them slow; the words get exercised either way.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we open at morning?" (the curtains) "What do we click at story time?" (the lamp) "What is warm under bare feet?" (the rug)

This lesson pairs with the Bedroom Objects flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Storage Words — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches storage as a home-for-everything: five words, five real homes in your house, and a game that turns tidy-up time into sending things back where they live.

What is this?

Storage is where things live when they are not being used: socks in the drawer, dishes in the cupboard, books on the shelf, toys in the basket, surprises in the box.

What does it mean?

Tidy-up time fails when putting away has no address. Once each thing has a named home, the child is not cleaning — the child is rehoming, which is a completely different feeling.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and five real storage homes your own house uses. Match the card where you can; the box can be any box — it is the most flexible member.

Why this matters

The word cupboard wears its passport openly: UK homes say cupboard, US homes say cabinet or closet. Say yours, offer the other, and the storage map works in both countries.

What it teaches

Organization logic (a place for everything), matching (thing to home), and the tidy-up identity — I am the person who sends things home.

Words to learn

drawercupboardcabinetshelfbasketboxstorage

Say this to your child

“"Storage words! Everything in this house lives somewhere. The spoon lives in the drawer, the teddy lives in the basket — let us send everybody home."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "five homes — let us meet the real ones in our house."
  2. Open the drawer together: one thing in, one thing out, say its address — "the drawer."
  3. Cupboard or cabinet: the dishes live here; open, look, close gently.
  4. Shelf and basket: one book home, one toy home, said out loud.
  5. The box last — "the box is the most generous home, it takes anything" — and tidy-up begins.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Storage Words" sit over an open drawer, a two-door cupboard, a three-tier shelf, a woven basket with handles and a lidded box.

Ask your child

"Where does the spoon live?" "Where does the teddy live?" "Which storage home takes anything at all?" (the box)

What your child can say or do

Your child might give every object an address all day — "sock, drawer!" — invent homes for things that lack them, or close every drawer in the house like a little landlord.

Out in the real world

Storage runs the whole world: the shop has shelves, the library has shelves, the car has a glove box. A child who knows storage words reads rooms everywhere.

Try it together

Send It Home: five things on the rug, five homes named. The child carries each one to its address — the last delivery gets a cheer. Pack away time is now the game, not the argument.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where do the dishes live?" (the cupboard — the cabinet) "Where do the toys live?" (the basket) "What is the word for where things live?" (storage)

This lesson pairs with the Storage Words flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Household Objects — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the soft furniture of belonging: the clock, the picture frame, the vase, the cushion and the curtain — the things nobody needs but every home keeps.

What is this?

Household objects are the small keepers of a home’s feeling: a clock to tick, a frame to hold a face, a vase to hold flowers, a cushion to hold a head, a curtain to hold the day out.

What does it mean?

These words carry feelings with them — the frame holds someone loved, the vase holds something grown. Vocabulary tied to affection is the vocabulary children keep.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and a slow walk through your own home, visiting the real versions. Each one gets its word and one sentence about what it holds or does.

Why this matters

This is the lesson where the child learns that homes are decorated on purpose — someone chose the frame, someone picked the flowers. Next comes "can we pick the flowers?"

What it teaches

Affective vocabulary (holds, keeps, loves), noticing detail (what is IN the frame?), and the cushion-curtain pair that appears in every soft room.

Words to learn

clockpicture framevasecushioncurtainhousehold

Say this to your child

“"Household objects — the keepers! The clock keeps the time, the frame keeps a face, the vase keeps the flowers, the cushion keeps your head, the curtain keeps the night."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "five things that make our house ours — let us visit them."
  2. The clock: hold a finger to your ear-watching, tick, tick — what is it saying?
  3. The frame: who is in it? Say the name — the frame holds people we love.
  4. The vase: are there flowers today? Whose room has one?
  5. Cushion and curtain to finish: one to lean on, one to close the day — both words said twice.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Household Objects" sit over a round clock, a standing picture frame, a blue-striped vase, a soft square cushion and blue curtains with tied-back ties.

Ask your child

"What does the clock do all day?" (tick — keep the time) "Who is inside our picture frame?" "What holds flowers?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might appoint the clock the house’s heartbeat, choose which picture earns the frame spot next, or arrange every cushion into a throne before sitting.

Out in the real world

Frames and vases appear at every grandparent’s house — and now the child can greet them by name and ask whose face that is. The words make visiting richer.

Try it together

Cushion Corner: build a reading corner with every cushion in the house, sit inside it, and name the household objects you can see from there. The softest vocabulary lesson available.

Understanding check

Ask: "What keeps the time?" (the clock) "What holds someone we love?" (the picture frame) "What closes the day at bedtime?" (the curtain)

This lesson pairs with the Household Objects flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Daily Routines — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the day as a five-step story the child already stars in: the chart is made together, and from then on the clothespin does the arguing.

What is this?

A daily routine is the order a day keeps: wake up, get dressed, eat breakfast, brush teeth, and at the far end, go to bed — the same order, every day.

What does it mean?

Routine is time made visible. A child who cannot read a clock can still read a clothespin on a chart, and the clothespin answers the only question that matters: what comes next?

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, a strip of paper, five quick drawings (or the card itself) and one clothespin. The chart goes at child height — its power is its reachability.

Why this matters

Transitions are where the day fights back. The chart moves the argument from person to object: not "get dressed because I said" but "the pin moved — it is dressing time."

What it teaches

Sequencing and time concepts, self-management (the child moves the pin), and the deep comfort of predictability — the day has a shape and the shape is friendly.

Words to learn

wake upget dressedbreakfastbrush teethgo to bedroutine

Say this to your child

“"Daily routines — the day has five doors! Wake up, dressed, breakfast, teeth, bed. You are the pin-mover: when the pin moves, the day moves."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "five steps make one day — here they are in order."
  2. Read each step with its gesture: stretch (wake up), arms up (get dressed), spoon (breakfast), big grin (brush teeth), hands together (go to bed).
  3. Make the chart: five pictures on a strip, the child decorates, the clothespin sits at step one.
  4. All day, the child moves the pin at each step — announce it proudly.
  5. At bedtime the pin rests on go-to-bed: "the pin finished the day. So did you."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Daily Routines" sit over five small scenes in order: a bed with the sun waking, folded clothes, a breakfast bowl with milk, a toothbrush and paste, and a bedtime bed with a moon in the window.

Ask your child

"What comes after breakfast?" (brush teeth) "What is the last step of the day?" (go to bed) "Who moves the pin?" (you do!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might move the pin before the step is done (and defend it fiercely), carry the chart around like a schedule, or ask where the pin goes at nap time.

Out in the real world

The five steps follow the child everywhere — holidays, weekends, grandma’s house. The pin can travel in a pocket; the routine comes with it.

Try it together

Routine Charades: act one step silently — the child guesses and then performs it. Brushing teeth pantomime is the family favorite. Five acts, five guesses, one whole day practiced.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many steps in our day?" (five) "What do we do after getting dressed?" (eat breakfast) "Who runs the chart?" (the child — the pin-mover)

This lesson pairs with the Daily Routines flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Bedroom Routines — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the bedroom’s day: five routines that happen in one room from morning to night, each one owned by the child who does it.

What is this?

The bedroom routines run twice daily: make the bed and open the curtains in the morning; get dressed, read the book and turn off the light at night.

What does it mean?

A made bed is the day’s first finished task and the room’s nightly welcome. Children who close their own day — book, light — sleep on a story that ended well.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, the bed and the curtains. The morning half takes three minutes; the night half is bedtime anyway — this lesson borrows it and names it.

Why this matters

Morning jobs done in the bedroom mean the room is already won before breakfast. And the night job is the lesson’s secret: turning off the light is the child saying the day is complete.

What it teaches

Task completion (pillows first, blanket up, done), daily responsibility, and the closing ritual that tells the body the day is over.

Words to learn

make the bedcurtainsget dressedreadturn off the light

Say this to your child

“"Bedroom routines! Morning: bed made, curtains open — the room is ready. Night: book read, light off — the room is sleeping. You ran the whole day in one room."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card in the morning: "the bedroom has jobs — here are all five."
  2. Make the bed together: pillows first, blanket up, corners as best they land. Announce it finished.
  3. Open the curtains: hello, day — the room is awake.
  4. At night, get dressed for bed, then the book: one story on the made bed.
  5. The child turns off the light — the fifth word, the last move, the room sleeps.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Bedroom Routines" sit over a bed being made, blue curtains opening on a window, a folded shirt and trousers, an open book and a bedside lamp with a hand reaching for the switch.

Ask your child

"What do we do first in the bedroom?" (make the bed) "What opens the morning?" (the curtains) "What is the very last thing at night?" (turn off the light)

What your child can say or do

Your child might make the bed with military pride and forbid all sitting on it, read the book aloud to the blanket, or turn the light off with a ceremonial flourish.

Out in the real world

The made bed follows the child to every sleepover and hotel — the job travels. So does the closing ritual: book, light, goodnight, wherever the pillow is.

Try it together

Room Flip: time the morning half — bed and curtains, together, from lights-on to done. Beat yesterday’s time by a smile, not a stopwatch. The room flips itself eventually.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we make in the morning?" (the bed) "What do we open?" (the curtains) "What closes the day?" (the light going off)

This lesson pairs with the Bedroom Routines flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Bathroom Words — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the bathroom at bath time, when every word on the card is working at full volume: water running, soap bubbling, towel waiting.

What is this?

The bathroom keeps the sink, the bath, the shower, the towel and the soap — the five big friends that every wash day needs.

What does it mean?

Bath time is the richest vocabulary hour of the day — warm, wet, daily and already loved. Words learned in the bath are learned for good.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and a real bath or shower. Each word is said at the moment its thing happens — soap is taught as soap is used.

Why this matters

The tap-faucet pair rides in naturally: the card says the water words, the family says whichever, and the child hears both without a lesson about countries.

What it teaches

Object vocabulary in real time, sensory anchoring (soap = slippery, towel = warm), and the sequencing of a wash — water, soap, rinse, dry.

Words to learn

sinkbathshowertowelsoaptapfaucetwater

Say this to your child

“"Bathroom words, live! The tap — some say faucet — brings the water, the soap makes the bubbles, the towel gives the hug. Hello to all five friends."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card as the bath fills: "five friends are here tonight — let us say hello to each."
  2. Sink first, hands in: the sink word with the tap (faucet) running.
  3. Soap: one pump or one rub, bubbles up — the word sticks to the slipperiness.
  4. Bath or shower — whichever tonight: name it as the water pours.
  5. Towel last, warm from the rack: wrap, and the five are all met.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Bathroom Words" sit over a pedestal sink with a tap, a claw-foot bath, a glass shower with the water running, a hanging towel and a dish of green soap.

Ask your child

"What makes the bubbles?" (the soap) "What brings the water?" (the tap — the faucet) "What hugs you dry?" (the towel)

What your child can say or do

Your child might pour for the toys while naming the whole bathroom, ask whether the shower or the bath is bigger, or demand the soap word again at every hand wash.

Out in the real world

Hotel bathrooms, swimming pools, grandparent houses — the five friends are always there. The child who met them at home greets them everywhere.

Try it together

Bath Band: each wash-day item gets a sound — tap goes drip, soap goes squidge, shower goes pssh, towel goes flap. The child plays the band while getting clean; the words rehearse themselves.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does the water come from?" (the tap — the faucet) "What do we scrub with?" (the soap) "What dries us?" (the towel)

This lesson pairs with the Bathroom Words flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

More Bathroom Words — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the bathroom’s remaining words — including the toilet ones — plainly and calmly, which is exactly how they stay useful.

What is this?

The rest of the bathroom: the bath mat under wet feet, the mirror above the sink, the toothbrush holder, the toilet and its paper.

What does it mean?

Toilet words said plainly stay plainly useful for life. A child who can say what they need without embarrassment asks for help sooner, in every bathroom in the world.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the real room. The mirror does the heavy lifting — it turns the lesson into a show — and the mat gets its word underfoot.

Why this matters

The holder is the surprise word: the child’s own toothbrush lives in a named place. And the mat carries the safety half — wet feet slip, mats catch them.

What it teaches

Body vocabulary said calmly, self-care independence, and mirror work — faces, teeth, hair — that rehearses every grooming skill there is.

Words to learn

bath matmirrortoothbrush holdertoilettoilet paper

Say this to your child

“"More bathroom words! The mat catches your feet, the mirror shows your grin, the holder keeps your brush — and the toilet words we say the same way we say all the others."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "the bathroom has more words — here are the last five."
  2. Step on the mat: how does it feel? That is its job — catching wet feet.
  3. Mirror time: show your teeth, make a happy face, a surprised face — the mirror shows everything back.
  4. Open the holder: whose brush lives here? Name the holder by name.
  5. Toilet words last, plainly: the toilet and the toilet paper — everybody uses them, every day.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "More Bathroom Words" sit over a bath mat, a rounded mirror, a cup holding two toothbrushes, a toilet with its lid down and a roll of toilet paper on its holder.

Ask your child

"What keeps wet feet from slipping?" (the bath mat) "What shows you your face?" (the mirror) "Where does your toothbrush live?" (the holder)

What your child can say or do

Your child might check the mirror after every face-wash, straighten the mat like a ringmaster, or teach the toilet words to a teddy in exactly your calm voice.

Out in the real world

Every bathroom away from home has the same five — the mat, the mirror, the holder, the toilet, the paper. New bathrooms stop being unknown when the words already fit.

Try it together

Mirror Show: two minutes of mirror games — happy, surprised, sleepy, silly — ending with the biggest tooth-brushing grin. The mirror rehearses faces; the words rehearse along.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we step on with wet feet?" (the mat) "What do we see ourselves in?" (the mirror) "Where does the toothbrush stand?" (the holder)

This lesson pairs with the More Bathroom Words flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Bathroom Routines — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the bathroom as five actions with five songs: the singing does the sequencing, and the child runs the whole routine on melody alone.

What is this?

The bathroom routines are the verbs of the room: wash hands, brush teeth, wash face, take a bath, dry hands — done daily, in some order, forever.

What does it mean?

Routines live on rails, and songs are rails. A two-line tune with the words inside — bubbles, bubbles, scrub and rinse — will outlast any reminder a grown-up can give.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and any sink. Invent the two-line songs together on the spot; familiar tunes (happy birthday speed) work better than clever ones.

Why this matters

Hand washing needs its twenty seconds — a song is the timer. Teeth need their two minutes — another song, longer. The music is not decoration; it is the mechanism.

What it teaches

Self-care sequences, timing by song (an early math sense), and the ownership of hygiene — the child who starts the song starts the routine.

Words to learn

wash handsbrush teethwash facetake a bathdry hands

Say this to your child

“"Bathroom routines — with the songs! Sing the hands song while the bubbles work, sing the teeth song while the brush runs. The music does the remembering."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "five jobs, five songs — let us write them."
  2. Hands song first, at the real sink: soap, bubbles, scrub, rinse — sing it twice through (that is the twenty seconds).
  3. Teeth song: up and down, front and back — long version, two minutes for the real brush.
  4. Face song at the wash: splish, tickle, done.
  5. Drying song to finish: towel, towel, dry dry dry — the forgotten half, now sung.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Bathroom Routines" sit over five small scenes: hands under a running tap, a brush and toothpaste in a cup, hands splashing a face, a bubble-topped bath and hands drying on a towel rail.

Ask your child

"What song goes with the soap?" "How long do we brush?" (the whole teeth song) "What comes after washing — always?" (drying)

What your child can say or do

Your child might sing the hands song at every random sink, conduct the teeth song with the brush, or assign the drying song to every towel in the house.

Out in the real world

The songs travel: any sink, any campsite, any grandparent’s bathroom — the child starts singing and the washing happens on beat. Restrooms everywhere run on this.

Try it together

Song Swap: tonight the child composes a new line for one routine song and teaches it to you. Composer-led hygiene: the routine gets renewed by its owner.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we sing while the soap bubbles?" (the hands song) "What is the forgotten half of washing?" (drying) "Who starts the songs?" (you do)

This lesson pairs with the Bathroom Routines flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Washing & Bathing — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches bath night item by item, with the toys as the rehearsal crew: what the child does to the teddy, the child accepts for themselves.

What is this?

Bath night uses its own kit: the shower gel for bubbles, the sponge for scrubbing, the bath towel for wrapping, the bath toys for morale and the hair dryer for warm endings.

What does it mean?

The toys are the mechanism: a child who scrubs a teddy’s back with the sponge has rehearsed sitting still for their own. Every wash-day item gets a rehearsal.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the real kit at the real bath. The hair dryer is demonstrated, not handed over: warm air, grown-up hands, the cool button as the child’s one press.

Why this matters

Equipping the bath turns waiting into doing — the child manages the toys’ wash while their own hair gets washed. The kit words carry the night.

What it teaches

Sequenced self-care, pretend-play as rehearsal for real care, and the body-map that comes from naming where the sponge goes — arms, tummy, back.

Words to learn

shower gelspongebath towelbath toyshair dryer

Say this to your child

“"Washing and bathing! Squirt the gel, scrub with the sponge — teddy first, then you. The towel hugs you out and the dryer hums you warm."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card as the water runs: "bath night has its own team — here they are."
  2. Shower gel: one squirt into the water, bubbles up — the word rides the smell.
  3. Sponge: the child scrubs the teddy first, then their own arms — arms, tummy, back, named.
  4. Toys washed and dried on the edge — the whole crew attends.
  5. Towel wrap at the end, and the hair dryer demo: warm air, one cool-button press, done.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Washing and Bathing" sit over a bottle of shower gel, a blue sponge, a hanging bath towel with a stripe, a rubber duck beside a toy boat and a hair dryer.

Ask your child

"What makes the bubbles in the water?" (the shower gel) "What do we scrub with?" (the sponge) "What wraps you after?" (the bath towel)

What your child can say or do

Your child might run a full wash-day for every toy, request the sponge by name each night, or press the cool button for every stuffed animal in the house.

Out in the real world

Swimming lessons, beach days and hotel baths all run on this kit — gel, towel, dry. A child who knows the words brings their own routine to any tub.

Try it together

Toy Wash Day: teddy and duck get the full service — gel, sponge, rinse, towel — narrated by the child. Then the child takes the same service. The order never changes: toys first.

Staying safe

The hair dryer is a grown-up tool, always: warm air only, never the hot setting near skin, cord clear of the water. The child presses the cool button; the grown-up holds the machine.

This lesson pairs with the Washing & Bathing flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Personal Care — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches personal care as ownership: the child’s own kit, the child’s own routine, and the one rule — personal means personal.

What is this?

Personal care is the care of your own body with your own tools: the toothbrush and toothpaste, the hairbrush and the comb, the tissue for any nose.

What does it mean?

Mine is the magic word of this lesson. A named, owned kit is a used kit — and the nobody-borrows rule teaches hygiene and boundaries in the same breath.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the real kit: brush, paste, hairbrush or comb (both if you have them), tissues. The kit gets a home of its own — that is the lesson’s anchor.

Why this matters

The brush-comb pair is a gentle first comparison: teeth different, hair different — two tools, two jobs. And the tissue completes the set for every nose in every season.

What it teaches

Self-care independence, hygiene rules (no sharing of personal tools), and sequence-ownership: the child runs their own two-minute routine.

Words to learn

toothbrushtoothpastehairbrushcombtissuepersonal

Say this to your child

“"Personal care — your kit, your routine! Brush and paste for the teeth, brush and comb for the hair, tissue for the nose. And the rule: personal tools are personal."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "this is a personal kit — yours, nobody else’s."
  2. Name each tool at its home: the brush and paste in the holder, the hairbrush and comb, the tissue box.
  3. Run the routine with the child leading: paste on, brush round, hair brushed or combed.
  4. Say the rule warmly: personal tools are not borrowed — nobody uses your brush, you use nobody’s.
  5. Tissue last: one blow, into the bin — the kit is complete.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Personal Care" sit over a blue-handled toothbrush, a tube of toothpaste, a paddle hairbrush, a wide-tooth comb and a blue tissue box with one tissue peeking out.

Ask your child

"Which tools are yours and nobody else’s?" "What does the comb do that the brush does too?" "Where does a used tissue go?" (in the bin)

What your child can say or do

Your child might guard the kit like a dragon, comb every doll’s hair with their own comb, or recite the nobody-borrows rule unprompted at the dentist.

Out in the real world

Sleepovers and hotel stays test the kit: a child with their own travel brush and comb keeps the routine anywhere. The rule follows the tools.

Try it together

Kit Check: at the morning routine, the child names their tools as they use them — brush, paste, brush, comb — and closes with the rule. Full kit named is a full kit used.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we put on the brush?" (the toothpaste) "What has wide teeth for tangles?" (the comb) "Who may use your toothbrush?" (nobody — it is personal)

This lesson pairs with the Personal Care flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Kitchen Actions — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the kitchen through its verbs: the room is not things but doings, and the child gets one doing to own each evening.

What is this?

The kitchen runs on actions: cook dinner, set the table, wash the dishes, open the fridge, pour a drink — the five verbs this card puts on display.

What does it mean?

Action words are the grammar of helping. A child who owns set-the-table has a role, not an assignment — and roles are what make a family engine run.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and any meal. The verbs are taught live: set the table as the table is set, pour as the water pours (small jug, big glass, steady hands).

Why this matters

One real verb per evening beats all the pretend cooking in the world. The child who sets the table tonight reads the verb card differently tomorrow.

What it teaches

Verb vocabulary, task persistence (a set table is a finished task), and the pour — a fine-motor classic that doubles as a patience lesson.

Words to learn

cookset the tablewash dishesfridgepourkitchen

Say this to your child

“"Kitchen actions! Cook, set, wash, open, pour — pick your verb for tonight. The table is waiting for its plate, cup and spoon."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card before dinner: "the kitchen is a room of verbs — you get one tonight."
  2. Read the five actions with their mime: stir, lay, scrub, open, pour.
  3. Assign tonight’s verb — setting the table is the best starter: plate, cup, spoon, named as they land.
  4. Open the fridge together: what does the fridge keep? Cold things — name two.
  5. Pour last: the child pours their own water from a small jug. Spills are data, not disasters.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Kitchen Actions" sit over five small scenes: a steaming pot on the stove, a laid place setting, a sink of dishes with bubbles, an open fridge full of food and a jug pouring a glass.

Ask your child

"What do we do before dinner lands?" (set the table) "What keeps the food cold?" (the fridge) "Which verb did you do tonight?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might assign verbs to the whole family like a head chef, pour everything in sight (water, oats, bath toys), or open the fridge just to greet the cold.

Out in the real world

Restaurants, cafés and grandma’s kitchen all run on the same five verbs. The child who sets tables at home sets them anywhere — and notices when nobody has.

Try it together

Verb Dice: five verbs on five paper squares, pick one blind each evening — that is tonight’s job. The draw is the ceremony; the doing is the lesson; the fridge-opening is always popular.

Staying safe

The stove and the oven are grown-up verbs — the child stirs only from a stool, with a grown-up beside and the pan handle turned inward. Say it with the cook verb, every time.

This lesson pairs with the Kitchen Actions flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Home Appliances — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches appliances by their sounds: whirr, pop, beep — the house is full of machine voices, and each one belongs to a named machine with its own rules.

What is this?

Home appliances are the machines that help: the television shows, the fan cools, the computer works, the toaster toasts, the iron presses.

What does it mean?

Machines with rules are the first machines: the toaster is everyone’s (with a grown-up), the iron is nobody’s (but a grown-up). Machine etiquette starts here and scales to everything with a plug.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and a sound hunt: which machines can you hear right now? The toaster demonstration is the finale — bread in, count, pop, toast.

Why this matters

Sound-first naming works because machines announce themselves: the child learns which whirr is the fan and which pop is the toaster, and the house becomes legible by ear.

What it teaches

Sound-object matching, machine safety categories (mine with help / grown-up only), and the anticipation-timing of the toaster countdown.

Words to learn

televisionfancomputertoasterironmachine

Say this to your child

“"Home appliances! The fan goes whirr, the toaster goes pop, the television says the story. Which machine is talking right now?"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "five machines help this house — let us hear them."
  2. Sound hunt first: sit still, which machines are talking? Fan? Fridge hum? Name what you find.
  3. Match the sounds to the card: whirr goes the fan, pop goes the toaster.
  4. Toaster demonstration with a grown-up: bread in, count together, pop — toast earned.
  5. The rules said kindly: the iron and the stove are grown-up machines; we look, we learn, we do not touch.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Home Appliances" sit over a wide television on its stand, an electric fan, a desktop computer with keyboard and mouse, a toaster with two slices and a blue iron.

Ask your child

"Which machine pops?" (the toaster) "Which machine cools us on hot days?" (the fan) "Which machines are grown-up only?" (the iron — and the stove)

What your child can say or do

Your child might announce every machine sound in the house like a sports commentator, count to pop with real faith, or ask what the computer is always working on.

Out in the real world

Every house hums with the same machines — hotels, holidays, grandparent visits. The child who knows the sounds can map any new house in one quiet minute.

Try it together

Machine Orchestra: the family assigns each heard machine a gesture — whirr (spin a finger), pop (jump), beep (tap a nose) — and plays the house as a symphony. The appliances teach themselves while you laugh.

Staying safe

Plugs and cords are grown-up territory, said with the words: machines get their power from the wall, and the wall side is never a child’s job. The toaster happens beside a grown-up, always.

This lesson pairs with the Home Appliances flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Shopping Words — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the shop before you get there: five words for the equipment of shopping, and a picture list that gives the child a job worth racing for.

What is this?

Shopping runs on its equipment: the shopping bag that carries, the basket for small trips, the trolley (the cart) for big ones, the wallet that pays, the receipt that proves.

What does it mean?

A child with a job at the shop is a partner, not cargo. The finder role — apples, bread, soap — converts aisle whining into aisle hunting, every single time.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, paper and a crayon for the picture list, and one real shop trip. The trolley-cart pair is said openly: same machine, two countries, two names.

Why this matters

The wallet-receipt pair teaches paying in two beats: money from the wallet, proof from the receipt. Abstract money grows a paper trail a child can hold.

What it teaches

List-reading (pictures before words), category hunting in a real environment, and the money script — pay, receipt, bag — rehearsed honestly.

Words to learn

shopping bagbasketreceiptwallettrolleyshopping cart

Say this to your child

“"Shopping words! Bag, basket, trolley — cart, if you like that word better. Wallet pays, receipt proves, and you — you are the finder today."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card before the trip: "the shop has equipment — learn it and you run it."
  2. Name the carry-crew: bag, basket, trolley — or cart, say both, pick your favorite out loud.
  3. Make the picture list together: three to five things, drawn by the child.
  4. At the shop: basket first, then the hunt — the child finds and crosses off.
  5. Wallet and receipt at the till: watch the pay, take the receipt, bag it up — the whole card, lived.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Shopping Words" sit over a blue shopping bag with a house mark, a woven basket, a paper receipt, a blue wallet and a wire trolley.

Ask your child

"What do we push at the big shop?" (the trolley — the cart) "What pays?" (the wallet) "What proves we paid?" (the receipt)

What your child can say or do

Your child might cross off list items with a flourish, choose cart or trolley as a personal identity, or demand the receipt like a tiny accountant.

Out in the real world

Every shop in every country runs this equipment — the words convert at the border (trolley to cart, receipt stays receipt). A child with a list shops happily in any language.

Try it together

Shop at Home: line up pantry goods, hand over the picture list, a basket and a toy wallet — the child shops the hallway. Real receipts optional; the pride is not.

Understanding check

Ask: "What carries the shopping home?" (the shopping bag) "What is the big wheeled one called?" (trolley — or cart) "Who was the finder today?" (the child)

This lesson pairs with the Shopping Words flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Cleaning & Tidying — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches cleaning as a trade with tools: five words, each tied to a real job a child can own — and the vacuum cleaner is the crown jewel.

What is this?

The cleaning kit has five members: the sponge for spills, the cloth for wiping, the spray bottle for wetting the wipe, the bin for the rubbish, the vacuum cleaner for the floors.

What does it mean?

Children do not want chores; they want tools. Give a child their own spray bottle (water only) and a cloth, and the table-wiping job applies for itself daily.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, a small cloth, a sponge and one empty spray bottle filled with water — labeled with the child’s name. The bin and the vacuum get the field trips.

Why this matters

Bin, trash can, garbage can — this lesson says all three once, then picks the family’s. The word matters less than the rule that rides with it: in the bin and it stays.

What it teaches

Tool-use skills (spray, wipe, scoop), sequence thinking (spray, then wipe, then bin), and work pride — the family floor looks better because of you.

Words to learn

spongeclothspray bottlebintrash canvacuum cleaner

Say this to your child

“"Cleaning and tidying — the tool kit! Spray, wipe, bin, and the big VRRROOM machine. You have your own bottle now; the table has been asking for you."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "cleaners have tools — today you get your own."
  2. Fill the spray bottle together: water only, name labeled, trigger practiced on the sink first.
  3. The table job: spray once, wipe with the cloth, fold and hang the cloth — the full professional sequence.
  4. Sponge to the bathroom sink: one spill, one press, wring it out — squeeze is the fun part.
  5. Vacuum finale: the child presses the switch, steers a straight line beside you, and the word VROOOM belongs to them.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Cleaning and Tidying" sit over a two-tone sponge, a folded blue cloth, a spray bottle with a trigger, a pedal bin and a canister vacuum cleaner with its hose.

Ask your child

"What do we spray on the table?" (water — only water) "What catches the crumbs?" "Which machine eats the dust?" (the vacuum cleaner)

What your child can say or do

Your child might spray everything except the table, demand the vacuum for every crumb in the postcode, or narrate the bin like a hungry monster being fed.

Out in the real world

Spills happen everywhere — restaurants, grandma’s, the car. A child with wipe skills becomes the designated helper, and helpers are never bored.

Try it together

Crumby Café: sprinkle cereal bits on a tray, and the child runs the whole cleanup — sweep to the dustpan, tip to the bin, wipe the tray. Restaurant closed, kitchen spotless, job very well done.

Staying safe

The spray bottle is WATER ONLY and lives apart from real cleaning products — say it plainly: grown-up cleaners are not for children, ever. The vacuum’s cord stays behind the child, and the bin stays unexplored.

This lesson pairs with the Cleaning & Tidying flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Cleaning Tools — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the big tools by their one jobs: each tool sweeps, washes or catches exactly one thing, and the child learns the whole assembly line.

What is this?

The floor-and-dust team: the broom sweeps, the mop washes, the bucket carries, the dustpan catches, the duster tickles the shelves.

What does it mean?

Tools with one clear job teach systems: crumbs are swept, then caught, then binned — a three-step pipeline a child can run end to end with nothing but pride.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the real tools, ideally a child-size broom or at least a personal dustpan. The duster is the instant hit — hand it over first.

Why this matters

The broom-mop distinction is the lesson’s brain-stretch: both have long handles, but one is for dry crumbs and one is for wet floors. Same shape, different job — thinking begins.

What it teaches

Tool-function matching, pipeline sequencing (sweep, catch, tip), and the fine grip of duster work — plus the dignity of real equipment, not toys.

Words to learn

broommopbucketdustpandustersweep

Say this to your child

“"Cleaning tools, one job each! The broom sweeps — swish. The dustpan catches — plop. The duster tickles — choo! Which tool do you want today?"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "five tools, five jobs — meet the team."
  2. Duster first: the child dusts one shelf, tickling everything once — instant success.
  3. Broom and dustpan: sweep crumbs toward the dustpan, catch, and tip them into the bin — the pipeline, run once.
  4. Mop and bucket: show how the mop drinks from the bucket, then washes one floor square — the wet half of the family.
  5. End with the one-job chant: brooms sweep, mops wash, dusters tickle.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Cleaning Tools" sit over a straw broom, a string mop, a blue bucket, a blue dustpan with its handle and a feather duster.

Ask your child

"Which tool washes the floor?" (the mop) "Which one catches the crumbs?" (the dustpan) "What does the duster do?" (tickles the shelves clean)

What your child can say or do

Your child might appoint themselves dust officer for life, sweep the same square for twenty happy minutes, or explain the one-job rule to visitors unprompted.

Out in the real world

Cafés, shops and school halls all have the same team standing in the corner. The child who knows the tools can identify the whole cleaning closet anywhere.

Try it together

Crumb Hunt: hide ten paper crumbs around one room; the child sweeps (hand broom or hand as broom), catches each in the dustpan and delivers them to the bin. Ten found, floor spotless, worker triumphant.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the broom do?" (sweeps) "What drinks from the bucket?" (the mop) "Where do the crumbs go after the dustpan?" (in the bin)

This lesson pairs with the Cleaning Tools flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Laundry Words — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches laundry as a journey the clothes take: dirty to bubbly to line to folded, with the child as the loader, the counter and the peg-clipping crew.

What is this?

Laundry words follow the wash: the washing machine tumbles, the detergent bubbles, the clothesline dries, the clothespins hold, the iron smooths.

What does it mean?

The machine is mesmerizing — round and round — and the child who loads it with you owns a piece of the magic. Washing line and pegs ride alongside clothesline and clothespin: same journey, two shores.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, one real load of washing, and (for the mini version) a string, two chairs and two pegs. The iron is demonstrated only, and from a safe distance.

Why this matters

Sorting colors is a real sorting game with a consequence — a red sock incident is a legend that teaches faster than any lecture. The child sorts; the family remembers.

What it teaches

Sorting by category (colors), measuring by counting (one scoop — the grown-up’s hand, the child’s count), sequencing a multi-day process, and peg work for little fingers.

Words to learn

washing machinedetergentclotheslinewashing lineclothespinpegiron

Say this to your child

“"Laundry words! The machine tumbles round and round, the detergent makes the bubbles, the line holds the clothes up in the sun. Clip the pegs — you are the clothes’ anchor."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card by the machine: "the clothes are going on a journey — here is the map."
  2. Sort with the child: colors with colors — darks here, lights there, and the story of why, told briefly.
  3. Load together: clothes in, detergent measured by the grown-up, counted by the child, door shut, start pressed.
  4. Watch the window a moment — round and round — then hang: line or rack, pegs (pins) clipped by small hands.
  5. The iron is the finale you only watch: warm plate, smooth moves, grown-up hands, wrinkle gone.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Laundry Words" sit over a front-loading washing machine mid-cycle, a bottle of detergent, a clothesline with a shirt and socks hanging, a wooden clothespin and a blue iron.

Ask your child

"Where do the clothes get clean?" (the washing machine) "What holds them on the line?" (the clothespin — the peg) "What makes the bubbles?" (the detergent)

What your child can say or do

Your child might guard the machine window like drive-in cinema, peg everything in reach (including curtains), or ask when the iron gets to be theirs.

Out in the real world

Every home in every country runs this journey — hotels have laundry chutes, holidays have laundromats. The child who knows the words narrates the whole trip.

Try it together

Mini Line: string between two chairs, two socks, two pegs — the child hangs the washing, takes it down, folds it into a basket. The whole journey in miniature, run by the smallest crew member.

Staying safe

Detergent is a grown-up pour — pods especially are never play things, and the box lives up high. The iron is look-don’t-touch until the far future: hot plate, grown-up hands, always.

This lesson pairs with the Laundry Words flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Outdoor Chores — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the outside jobs: the path, the plants, the leaves, the birds and the car — chores that wear costumes of play and work just as hard.

What is this?

Outdoor chores keep the home’s outside alive: sweep the path, water the plants, pick up the leaves, feed the birds, wash the car.

What does it mean?

Water is the hinge of this whole lesson: watering cans, buckets, sponges and hoses are chore tools and toy boxes at once. The work gets done because the water is wonderful.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, a small watering can, a bucket with a sponge, and a patch of path or leaves. The birds need only a feeder or a sprinkle of seeds and some quiet.

Why this matters

Feeding the birds is the empathy chore: something alive depends on the showing up. And leaf-piles are the only chore with a built-in celebration clause — jump first, bag second.

What it teaches

Gross-motor work (sweeping, scrubbing circles), care for living things, and the outside-in rhythm of a job with a natural finish — the path is clean, the car is shiny.

Words to learn

sweep the pathwater the plantspick up leavesfeed the birdswash the car

Say this to your child

“"Outdoor chores! Sweep the path, water the plants, pile the leaves, feed the birds — and the car gets its bath. Everything outside drinks or shines today."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card outside: "five jobs — all of them better than inside jobs."
  2. Sweep the path together: long strokes, one direction, leaves gather like magic.
  3. Water the plants: glug, glug — one can, many pots, count as you go.
  4. Leaf pile: gather, jump (mandatory), then bag — celebration is part of the pipeline.
  5. Birds and car to close: seeds sprinkled quietly, then the bubbly circles on the car — the sponge and bucket finale.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Outdoor Chores" sit over five small scenes: a broom sweeping a path, a watering can over a potted plant, a rake and leaf pile, a birdhouse and bird by a feeder, and a soapy car mid-wash.

Ask your child

"Who do we feed in the morning?" (the birds) "What do the plants drink?" (water from the can) "Which chore lets you jump in the pile first?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might water the same plant until it swims, choreograph a leaf-pile jump routine, or stand sentry at the bird feeder shushing the whole street.

Out in the real world

The same five jobs exist at every grandparent’s and every holiday rental: paths, plants, birds, cars. A child with outdoor-chore skills is welcome everywhere.

Try it together

Water the Circuit: five cups of water, five thirsty things — a plant, the bird bath, the car’s one panel, the path’s one corner, the child’s own hands. The circuit runs until the cups are empty and the job is genuinely done.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do the plants drink from?" (the watering can) "What do the birds eat?" (the seeds) "What do we do before we bag the leaves?" (jump in the pile)

This lesson pairs with the Outdoor Chores flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Garden Tools — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the garden’s team: five tools, each with a one-job rule, and the trowel handed to the child as their very own shovel.

What is this?

The garden runs on its tools: the shovel digs deep, the rake gathers, the trowel plants, the gloves guard the hands, the wheelbarrow hauls it all.

What does it mean?

Real tools, honestly given, are how children join the work. A child with their own trowel is not watching gardening — the child is gardening.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the real tools. The digging job is one pot or one small patch: trowel, hole, seed or seedling, done. Gloves go on first, every time — that is the ritual.

Why this matters

The yard-garden word rides along quietly: US families say yard, UK families say garden, the tools are identical. The one-job rule (shovels dig, rakes gather) is the lesson’s spine.

What it teaches

Tool discipline (one job each), fine and gross motor work (trowel grip, rake pull), and the sequence of planting — dig, place, cover, water.

Words to learn

shovelraketrowelgardening gloveswheelbarrowgardenyard

Say this to your child

“"Garden tools! Shovel digs, rake gathers, trowel plants — the trowel is YOUR little shovel. Gloves on, one hole to dig, and the wheelbarrow waits for its driver."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card outside: "the garden has a tool team — gloves first."
  2. Gloves on: the ritual that says work is beginning — wiggle each finger home.
  3. Meet the big tools by sight: the shovel digs deep holes, the rake gathers leaves — rrrike.
  4. The trowel is yours: one pot, one small hole, one seedling or seed in, soil patted down.
  5. Wheelbarrow finale: load the pots or leaves in, and the child takes one ride as the foreman.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Garden Tools" sit over a blue shovel, a rake, a hand trowel, a pair of cream gardening gloves and a blue wheelbarrow with one wheel.

Ask your child

"Which tool digs the small holes?" (the trowel) "What do we put on first?" (the gloves) "Which tool carries everything?" (the wheelbarrow)

What your child can say or do

Your child might sleep with the trowel, rake every leaf in the postcode into one noble pile, or ride the wheelbarrow and refuse to disembark.

Out in the real world

Community gardens, farms and grandma’s yard all run the same team. The child who knows trowel from shovel is handed real jobs at every garden gate.

Try it together

Tool Race (gentle edition): three picture cards — shovel, rake, trowel — and three jobs called out. The child runs to touch the right real tool. Digging bonus: one real hole in one real pot, dug entirely by them.

Staying safe

Tools are for their jobs and only their jobs, and the pointy ends stay down and away. The wheelbarrow ride happens with a grown-up steering. Gloves are the ritual that starts every session.

This lesson pairs with the Garden Tools flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Tools & Fix-It — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the fixing kit with its one rule riding alongside: tools are for fixing, real tools are used with a grown-up — and the hammer gets its honest debut.

What is this?

The fix-it team: the hammer drives nails, the screwdriver twists screws, the saw cuts (grown-ups only), and the toolbox is the home that latches them all in.

What does it mean?

Curiosity about tools is not misbehavior — it is engineering interest with nowhere to go. One real hammering session, goggles on, is worth a year of don’t-touch.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, a small hammer, a block of scrap wood, two nails started by you, and child-size goggles if you have them. The saw and the screwdriver stay demonstrated.

Why this matters

The toolbox latch is the lesson’s quiet star: tools live in their home and come out for jobs. The click of the latch closing is the ritual ending of every fix-it session.

What it teaches

Hammer control (aim, swing, follow-through), respect for edged tools, and the fix-it identity — broken things are projects, not tragedies.

Words to learn

hammerscrewdriversawtoolboxnailsfix

Say this to your child

“"Tools and fix-it! The hammer goes bang, the screwdriver goes twist, the saw is a grown-up machine. Today YOU are the fixer — goggles on, one nail at a time."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "the fix-it team sleeps in the toolbox — let us meet them."
  2. Open the toolbox together and name everyone: hammer, screwdriver, saw — each with its one job.
  3. Hammer debut: goggles on, nails started by the grown-up, the child drives them in — real wood, real sound, real pride.
  4. Screwdriver turn: one big screw in a soft block, twist, twist, twist.
  5. The saw is only waved at: back and forth motion in the air, and the rule said kindly — saws are grown-up tools, always.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Tools and Fix-It" sit over a claw hammer with a pink grip, a red-handled screwdriver, a hand saw, and a latched two-tier toolbox.

Ask your child

"Which tool goes bang?" (the hammer) "Which tool twists?" (the screwdriver) "Where do the tools sleep?" (the toolbox — latched)

What your child can say or do
