Your child might carry the goggles everywhere for a week, fix toys that were never broken, or close the toolbox latch with the gravity of a master mechanic.

Out in the real world

The fix-it instinct lasts: a child who has hammered real nails builds, repairs and helps for years. Every parent of a teenager with a flat-pack wardrobe thanks this lesson.

Try it together

Fix-It Clinic: gather one squeaky toy, one loose screw, one wobbly thing (all pre-approved) — the child diagnoses, you assist, the hammer or screwdriver does its true job, the latch clicks shut. Clinic closed.

Staying safe

Real tools, one rule, said the same way every time: tools come out for fixing, with a grown-up, and go home to the toolbox after. The saw is demonstrated in the air and never nearer. Goggles first, hammer second.

This lesson pairs with the Tools & Fix-It flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

More Tools — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson goes deeper into the toolbox for children who already know the basics: three grip-and-turn tools, one measuring friend, and the rule about pointy things.

What is this?

The deeper toolbox: the drill spins, the pliers grip, the wrench turns big bolts, the ruler measures, and the nails wait pointy side down.

What does it mean?

The ruler is the gateway tool: it measures anything, hurts nobody, and quietly teaches numbers. Give a child a ruler and they will measure the house — that is not a bug.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and a real ruler (paper or wooden). The drill is a demonstration at most — unplugged, trigger untouched — and the pliers and wrench are shown gripping, not wielded.

Why this matters

Grip-think is the new idea here: pliers grip, wrenches turn, and both hold things so hands do not have to. Plus the safety rhyme of the set: pointy things point down.

What it teaches

Measurement sense (longer, shorter, how many), tool-function matching, and the grown-up-only categories said with warmth rather than worry.

Words to learn

drillpliersrulernailswrenchmeasure

Say this to your child

“"More tools! Pliers grip, the wrench turns, the drill spins for the grown-ups — and the ruler? The ruler measures EVERYTHING. Starting with your shoe."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "more tools for bigger jobs — and one friend for measuring."
  2. The ruler first, into the child’s hands: measure a shoe, a spoon, a book — numbers happen by themselves.
  3. Pliers demo: grip a soft sponge — squeeze, hold, release. That is their whole magic: gripping.
  4. Wrench: fit it over a big bolt (or a jar lid, safely still) — turn is the job.
  5. Drill: unplugged, shown spinning nothing — bzzzzt in the story, grown-up in the house. Nails last: pointy side down, always.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "More Tools" sit over a power drill, pliers with blue grips, a wooden ruler marked with numbers, a scatter of nails and a wide wrench.

Ask your child

"Which tool grips?" (the pliers) "Which tool measures?" (the ruler) "Which way do the nails point in the tin?" (pointy side down)

What your child can say or do

Your child might measure the cat (with negotiations), grip everything with two fingers like pliers, or declare the drill the loudest tool in the book.

Out in the real world

Measuring is everywhere — shops, post offices, craft tables. The child with a ruler and the habit of asking how-long has a math tool that fits in a pencil case.

Try it together

Measure the House: the ruler and a notebook, five things to measure — shoe, book, spoon, teddy, doorway. The child measures, you write the numbers, the notebook becomes the house’s first survey.

Staying safe

The drill is a grown-up machine, unplugged when shown. Nails point down and travel nowhere. And the tool-home rule holds: every tool returns to the toolbox, latch clicked.

This lesson pairs with the More Tools flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

By the Door — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the door zone by building it: a hook, a basket and a mat, with every word on the card assigned to a real place your child owns.

What is this?

By the door lives the going-out kit: the key that unlocks, the doormat that wipes, the umbrella for rain, the hat for sun, the shoes pointing out.

What does it mean?

Mornings collapse in the doorway. A launchpad with named places — shoes there, coat there, umbrella there — turns the exit into a checklist the child can run without a grown-up chasing.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, one hook (or one clear spot), one basket and the real shoes. The doormat and the key are taught where they actually are: at the actual door.

Why this matters

The key carries the safety word: keys are grown-up treasure, high up, never play. Said with the word, every time, and the rule needs no second lesson.

What it teaches

Organization by place (a home for the going-out things), self-dressing skills (shoes on at the mat), and weather-thinking — hat for sun, umbrella for rain.

Words to learn

keydoormatumbrellahatshoedoor

Say this to your child

“"By the door — the launchpad! Shoes at the mat, toes out. Hat on its hook. Umbrella waits for rain. Wipe, wipe, wipe — and we are off!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card at the front door: "everything that helps us leave lives HERE."
  2. The doormat: wipe, wipe, wipe — the mat’s one job, demonstrated twice, adopted forever.
  3. Shoes at the mat: toes pointing out, ready to slide in — the child sits, puts them on, done.
  4. Hook or basket: hat and umbrella get their home — sun hat here, rain umbrella there.
  5. The key goes high: where it lives, why it lives there, and whose job it is (the grown-up’s).

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "By the Door" sit over a golden key, a striped doormat, a folded blue umbrella, a blue hat with a green band and a lace-up sneaker.

Ask your child

"What do we wipe our feet on?" (the doormat) "What waits for a rainy day?" (the umbrella) "Whose job is the key?" (the grown-up’s — it lives up high)

What your child can say or do

Your child might wipe feet on every mat in town, stage umbrella drills on sunny days, or line up the family’s shoes with toes out like a parking lot.

Out in the real world

Every doorway has this zone — school entrances, swimming pools, grandma’s hall. The launchpad habit makes the child the smoothest leaver in any building.

Try it together

Launch Check: before any outing, the child runs the checklist aloud at the real door — shoes (toes out), hat if sunny, umbrella if gray, wipe the mat — and rings an imaginary bell when ready. Countdown to departure, run by the smallest officer.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where do the shoes wait?" (by the mat, toes out) "What unlocks the door?" (the key — a grown-up’s) "What does the mat do?" (wipes our feet)

This lesson pairs with the By the Door flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Letters & Parcels — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the mail by running it: one real letter, drawn and addressed by the child, posted with ceremony — and then the best part, the daily check.

What is this?

The mail equipment: the letter with words on paper, the envelope as its coat, the stamp as its ticket, the parcel as the box of surprises, and the mailbox where everything knocks.

What does it mean?

Mail is slow magic — you post it, you wait, and someday something comes back. The waiting trains patience; the checking builds a daily ritual; the parcel-package pair rides along in both accents.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, paper, crayons, an envelope, a real stamp and a real mailbox or post box within walking distance. The return address can be grandma — someone will write back.

Why this matters

The stamp is the wonder-word: a tiny sticker that is really a ticket for travel. And the arrival rule is gentle but firm — the mail belongs to the family, opened together.

What it teaches

Mark-making with real purpose (a letter someone will read), address awareness (our street, our number), and delayed gratification — the finest kind, with a postal service.

Words to learn

letterenvelopeparcelpackagestampmailboxpost

Say this to your child

“"Letters and parcels! The letter wears its envelope coat, the stamp buys the ride, and the mailbox takes it from there. Now we wait — and waiting for post is the best kind of waiting."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "this is how the world knocks on our door — in paper."
  2. Make the letter: the child draws; you write a real address on the envelope together.
  3. The stamp goes on top — its ticket — and the name reads like a spell.
  4. The walk to the mailbox: post it, wave, and the ceremony is complete.
  5. From then on, the daily check is the child’s: any post today? Anything with MY name on it?

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Letters and Parcels" sit over a lined letter, a cream envelope, a taped cardboard parcel, a portrait stamp and a blue mailbox on a post with its flag up.

Ask your child

"What carries the letter to grandma?" (the envelope — and the stamp, and the post) "What is a parcel?" (a box of surprises — a package) "Whose job is opening the mail?" (the family’s — together)

What your child can say or do

Your child might post drawings to everyone they know, check the mailbox twice before breakfast, or address envelopes to the cat.

Out in the real world

Post offices, birthday cards, library notices — the mail runs the world quietly. A child who posts a letter has joined a system that works in every country on Earth.

Try it together

Post Office: a shoebox counter, paper, envelopes, sticker stamps — the family posts drawings to each other all afternoon. The delivery walk (room to room, very official) completes the loop.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is the letter’s coat called?" (the envelope) "What buys the ride?" (the stamp) "Where does everything knock?" (the mailbox)

This lesson pairs with the Letters & Parcels flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Outside the Home — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the in-between places — not quite house, not quite street: the balcony, the gate, the path, the porch — and the two rules that live out there.

What is this?

Between the front door and the world lie the edges of home: the balcony up in the air, the gate that clicks, the mailbox on its post, the path that wanders, the porch that waves.

What does it mean?

Edges are where homes say this-far. A child who can name the edges — gate, balcony, path — can also be given their rules precisely, and precise rules hold.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and a slow walk of your own frontage: door to gate to path and back. If your home has a balcony, it gets visited; if not, a window ledge counts.

Why this matters

The two edge rules are taught on location, kindly: balconies are for holding a grown-up’s hand, and gates click shut behind us. Rules at the edge feel like facts, not lectures.

What it teaches

Spatial mapping (near, far, up, along), boundary understanding, and the porch-sit habit — the calmest watching game a family can own.

Words to learn

balconygatemailboxpathporchoutsideedge

Say this to your child

“"Outside the home! The path walks us to the gate, the gate clicks shut behind us, and the porch is where we wave. The edges of home are the best seats for watching the world."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card at the front door: "the home has edges — let us walk them."
  2. Out the door: is there a porch or step? Stand on it — this is where we wave goodbye.
  3. Follow the path: the path has a job — it shows us the way to the gate.
  4. The gate: open it together, then click it shut behind — the rule, said on the spot.
  5. Balcony (or the high window): look at it from below and say the hand-holding rule — then mailbox, and home again.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Outside the Home" sit over a blue balcony with railings, a double gate between posts, a blue mailbox, a stepping-stone path and a porch with a small roof.

Ask your child

"What walks us from door to gate?" (the path) "What do we do behind a gate?" (click it shut) "Where do we stand to wave goodbye?" (the porch)

What your child can say or do

Your child might click every gate in the neighborhood shut with pride, perform porch waves for departing guests, or point out paths wherever you walk.

Out in the real world

Parks, schools and libraries all have gates and paths — and the rules travel with the words. A child who clicks gates at home clicks them everywhere.

Try it together

Porch Sit: five minutes on the steps or at the window, naming everything that passes — a bird, a gate, a car, a cloud. Quiet voices, no toys, just watching. The oldest game there is.

Staying safe

Two edge rules, said kindly and on location: balconies and high places mean a grown-up hand, always — and gates click shut behind us. The rules belong to the words and come out with them.

This lesson pairs with the Outside the Home flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Outdoor Home Words — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the living edges of home: the fence that draws the circle, the bench that holds two, the feeder and the flower bed that make the yard a habitat.

What is this?

The outdoor home words: the fence, the bench, the bird feeder, the watering can and the flower bed — the green team that makes outside feel like yours.

What does it mean?

A yard (or garden) is a child’s first habitat, and these are its landmarks. Naming them turns the outside from a place you play into a place you keep.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the real outside — any fence counts, any bench, any flower. The bird feeder job works with a feeder, a windowsill tray or a handful of seeds.

Why this matters

The refill ritual is the lesson’s engine: birds visit the feeder that gets filled, flowers open in the bed that gets watered — and the child keeps both calendars.

What it teaches

Care for habitat (birds, plants), the boundary sense (the fence says this-far), and the observation habit — who visited today? What opened overnight?

Words to learn

fencebenchbird feederwatering canflower bedyardgarden

Say this to your child

“"Outdoor home words! The fence draws our circle, the bench holds two, the feeder feeds the birds and the flower bed drinks. Our outside is a habitat — and we are the keepers."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card outside: "our outside has its own words — let us meet them."
  2. The fence: walk it from one end to the other — this is the circle of our yard. Some say garden, some say yard: both are this patch.
  3. The bench: sit on it together — two seats, one view.
  4. The feeder refill: seeds in, hung where the birds trust, then step back and shush.
  5. The flower bed and the can: one glug per flower, and tomorrow there will be news.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Outdoor Home Words" sit over a pale picket fence, a wooden bench with blue trim, a hanging bird feeder with seeds, a blue watering can and a round flower bed with blooms.

Ask your child

"What draws the circle of the yard?" (the fence) "What do we fill for the birds?" (the bird feeder) "What holds two people?" (the bench)

What your child can say or do

Your child might keep a mental list of every bird that visited, water the fence (it does not mind), or sit the whole family on the bench one by one to test it.

Out in the real world

Parks and school yards have the same landmarks — fences, benches, feeders, beds. The child who knows them reads every outdoor space like a map.

Try it together

Who Came Today: each morning, one look at the feeder and one entry in the bird notebook — a drawing, a tally, a story. By week’s end the child knows their yard’s regulars by heart.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the fence say?" (this far — the circle of the yard) "What holds the seeds?" (the bird feeder) "Where do the flowers live?" (the flower bed)

This lesson pairs with the Outdoor Home Words flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Pets at Home — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the pets and their manners: the golden rule first — gentle, quiet, let them sleep — then the words, then the jobs.

What is this?

The pets at home: the cat, the dog, the fish bowl, the rabbit and the pet bed — the family members with fur and fins.

What does it mean?

Pets are the first someone-smaller-than-you a child learns to care for. The rule order matters: gentle before naming, naming before jobs — the respect is load-bearing.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and any pets in reach — your own, a neighbor’s, or the card alone. The golden rule is rehearsed before any paw is touched: gentle, quiet, let them sleep.

Why this matters

The pet bed rule looks small and is not: the pet’s place is the pet’s, like the child’s bed is the child’s. Respect for territory scales up to siblings and friends.

What it teaches

Gentle-touch practice (one finger stroke), reading animal signals (tail tells the truth), and care routines — food scoop, fresh water — sized to be genuinely helpful.

Words to learn

catdogfish bowlrabbitpet bedgentle

Say this to your child

“"Pets at home! The cat naps, the dog wags, the fish swims circles. Our rule comes first: gentle hands, quiet voices, let them sleep. Then — the food scoop. That is your job now."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "the smallest family members — with the biggest characters."
  2. The golden rule, said together: gentle hands, quiet voices, we let pets sleep.
  3. Practice the one-finger stroke on your own arm — that is pet-touch size.
  4. Meet the pets by name: the card’s cat, dog, rabbit, fish — and the real ones if you have them, each with their word.
  5. One pet job, sized small: the food scoop or the water bowl — done once, done gently, done again tomorrow.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Pets at Home" sit over a striped cat sitting tall, a spotted dog with a wagging tail, a goldfish in a round fish bowl with a plant, a cream rabbit and a pet bed with a paw print.

Ask your child

"What is the golden rule of pets?" (gentle, quiet, let them sleep) "Where does the fish live?" (the fish bowl) "Whose place is the pet bed?" (the pet’s)

What your child can say or do

Your child might shush the whole house for a napping cat, scoop pet food with enormous ceremony, or explain the golden rule to visitors at the door.

Out in the real world

Every pet you meet wears the same rule — friends’ dogs, farm cats, class rabbits. The child who learned gentle-hands at home is trusted with every animal after.

Try it together

Vet Practice: teddy is the patient; the child runs the gentle check — one-finger stroke, quiet voice, let him rest, food and water nearby. Then swap: the child is the pet, you are the gentle vet. Both sides learn the rule.

Understanding check

Ask: "How do we touch a pet?" (one finger, gentle) "What do we do when the pet sleeps?" (let them sleep) "Whose place is the pet bed?" (the pet’s own)

This lesson pairs with the Pets at Home flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Sounds at Home — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the house’s voices by listening for them: one quiet minute, a count of sounds, and a rule attached to the two that matter most.

What is this?

The home speaks in sounds: the doorbell announces, the telephone rings, the radio sings, the headphones hush, the alarm wakes.

What does it mean?

Sound words carry rules — doorbell means come together, alarm means up we get — and rules attached to sounds are the fastest ones children learn. The ears do the teaching.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and one quiet minute. The listen-hunt needs nothing else: the house is already performing. If the doorbell never rings, ring it yourself — once, by arrangement.

Why this matters

The doorbell rule is safety and manners in one: a visitor is met with a grown-up, every time. Said calmly with the word, it never needs to be said in a panic.

What it teaches

Auditory discrimination (which sound is which), sound-meaning mapping, and the quiet-minute discipline that makes listening a skill rather than an accident.

Words to learn

doorbelltelephoneheadphonesradioalarmsound

Say this to your child

“"Sounds at home — listen! Ding-dong means a visitor: we go to the door TOGETHER. The alarm means morning. What is the house saying right now?"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "our house has five voices — let us hear them."
  2. The quiet minute: sit, close eyes half-way, count the sounds you hear on your fingers.
  3. Match what you heard to the card — a hum, a tick, a car outside.
  4. The two big voices: the doorbell (who is it? we go together) and the alarm (time to wake).
  5. The headphone rule: music just for you — quiet ears, quiet room, everyone happy.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Sounds at Home" sit over a doorbell chime with a bell mark, a push-button telephone, blue headphones, a transistor radio with its dial and an alarm clock with twin bells.

Ask your child

"What does ding-dong mean?" (a visitor — we go together) "What wakes us up?" (the alarm) "What keeps music just for you?" (the headphones)

What your child can say or do

Your child might run to the door for every imaginary ding-dong, hold the headphones to your ears to share, or sleep-test the alarm with deep suspicion.

Out in the real world

Every building speaks — hotels, grandma’s, holiday lets. The child who knows the doorbell rule greets every strange doorbell exactly the same way: with a grown-up.

Try it together

Sound Detective: the child closes their eyes; you make one house sound — tap the door (knock knock), ring a bell, hum the radio. The detective names it and points at the card. Five rounds, one sharp-eared winner.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who goes to the doorbell?" (everyone — with a grown-up) "What sings in the kitchen?" (the radio) "What keeps the music just for one?" (the headphones)

This lesson pairs with the Sounds at Home flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Sounds Around Home — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the house’s self-made soundtrack: the sounds nobody switches on, from footsteps to creaks to drips — and the news each one carries.

What is this?

The sounds around home: footsteps tip-tapping, the door’s creak, the clock’s tick, the tap’s running (the faucet, across the ocean), the phone’s ring.

What does it mean?

Sound-reading is a safety skill wearing a game’s clothes: footsteps say who is coming, a running tap says somebody left it on, a creak says which door. Ears that read the house are useful ears.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the performing house. Every item can also be performed by body: march the footsteps, groan the creak, tick-tock the tongue, drip the fingers.

Why this matters

The tap-faucet pair returns here in its splashiest form: a running tap is the house’s loudest news. And the body-performance games make the words physical.

What it teaches

Sound-source reasoning (what made THAT?), onomatopoeia play (tip-tap, creak, tick-tock), and the detective habit of asking what the sound means.

Words to learn

footstepscreaky doorticking clockrunning tapringing phone

Say this to your child

“"Sounds around home! Tip-tap, creak, tick-tock, drip-drip, ring-ring — the house talks all day. What is it telling us right now?"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "the house plays music all day — here is the band."
  2. Perform each sound with your body: tip-tap feet, creeeak voice, tick-tock tongue, drip-drip fingers, ring-ring hands.
  3. Listen for real: which band member is playing right now? The clock is almost certainly on stage.
  4. The news game: what does a running tap say? (turn me off!) What do footsteps say? (someone is coming!)
  5. The tap check: is any tap dripping in the house? One walk, one listening tour, one hero.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Sounds Around Home" sit over two blue footprints, an open door with motion lines by its hinge, a round ticking clock, a tap with a drop falling and a vintage phone mid-ring.

Ask your child

"What do footsteps tell us?" (someone is coming) "What does a running tap say?" (turn me off) "What says tick-tock all night?" (the clock)

What your child can say or do

Your child might announce every creak in the building, patrol the house for dripping taps like a plumber-in-chief, or perform the whole band on request.

Out in the real world

The listening habit lasts: a child who reads house sounds reads street sounds, classroom sounds, nature sounds. Ears trained at home stay trained.

Try it together

House Orchestra: the family performs the five sounds in a loop — footsteps, creak, tick-tock, drip, ring — faster and faster until it collapses into giggles. Then the quiet-minute hunt for the real versions.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does creeeak mean?" (a door is opening) "What is the tap saying when it runs?" (turn me off) "Who makes tip-tap?" (the footsteps — someone walking)

This lesson pairs with the Sounds Around Home flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Technology at Home — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the glowing family by their jobs: the computer works, the tablet taps, the camera clicks, the headphones hush — and the charger, the child’s own job, feeds them all.

What is this?

Technology at home: the computer on its desk, the tablet in small hands, the headphones, the charger with its cable, the camera that says cheese.

What does it mean?

Machines that get fed are machines that work — and feeding them is a job a four-year-old can run perfectly. Ownership of one real tech job beats a hundred screen rules.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the real machines. The charger job needs a reachable plug and a bedtime slot; the camera gets one supervised click; the rules come with the words.

Why this matters

The tech manners ride with the names: tablets live where everyone can see, cameras ask before they click, screens sleep in the kitchen at night. Said calmly with the words, they hold.

What it teaches

Machine-care responsibility (charging is real maintenance), tech vocabulary, and the ask-before-clicking etiquette that scales to every camera the child will ever meet.

Words to learn

computertabletheadphoneschargercamerascreen

Say this to your child

“"Technology at home! The computer works, the tablet taps, the camera says cheese — and you, you are the charger. Machines that get fed at night work in the morning."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "the glowing machines — every one has a job."
  2. Meet them by job: the computer works, the tablet plays and learns, the camera remembers, the headphones hush.
  3. Charger duty, installed: at bedtime the child finds the tablet, brings it to the plug, and the grown-up connects — feeding time announced.
  4. Camera etiquette: one supervised photo — and the rule, cameras ask before they click.
  5. The sleeping rule: screens sleep in the kitchen at night — said like a fact about machines, which it is.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Technology at Home" sit over a desktop computer with keyboard and mouse, a tablet standing upright, blue headphones, a charger plug with its coiled cable and a compact camera.

Ask your child

"Which machine works at the desk?" (the computer) "What do machines eat?" (their power — from the charger) "What does a camera do before it clicks?" (it asks)

What your child can say or do

Your child might tuck the tablet in beside the charger like a teddy, narrate feeding time to the whole house, or demand the camera ask permission of everything.

Out in the real world

Every home runs on these machines — and on the small rituals that keep them alive. A child with charger duty understands power, plugs and patience before any screen-time debate begins.

Try it together

Tech Care Station: set up a bedtime charging shelf — one plug, one spot, one job. The child runs the whole routine: find, carry, plug (with you), announce. The machines sleep; the job is real.

Staying safe

Plugs and wall sockets are grown-up hands: the child finds and carries, the grown-up connects. Screens live in family rooms, not bedrooms — said with the words, every night.

This lesson pairs with the Technology at Home flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Safe at Home — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches safety as geography: the child learns where the safe things live, because knowing where safety lives is the first skill of being safe.

What is this?

The safe-at-home team: the first-aid box for bumps, the helmet for wheels, the key up high, the light switch, and the handwash at every sink.

What does it mean?

Safety tours done calmly make safety ordinary. A child who has peeked inside the first-aid box on a normal Tuesday is not frightened of it on the day it is needed.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the real locations: the first-aid box, the helmet, the sinks. Nothing is opened in an emergency mood — this is a tour, not a drill.

Why this matters

The kit-box pair rides here too — box in the UK, kit in the US, the same brave little container. And the keys rule comes attached: grown-up treasure, up high, never play.

What it teaches

Location memory (where does safety live?), hygiene habits (handwash at every sink), and the calm-fact tone that keeps safety from becoming scary.

Words to learn

first-aid boxfirst-aid kithelmetkeylight switchhandwash

Say this to your child

“"Safe at home — the guardians! The first-aid box waits for bumps, the helmet waits for wheels, the handwash waits at every sink. You know where safety lives now."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "our home has guardians — let us visit them all."
  2. The first-aid box: open it together — plasters, cream, the family phone list. Say where it lives and put it back.
  3. The helmet: try it on — helmets go on before wheels, bikes and scooters alike.
  4. The handwash: one pump at the real sink — where it lives, when we use it.
  5. The light switch and the key: lights off when we leave a room; keys up high, grown-up treasure.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Safe at Home" sit over a first-aid box with a red cross, a cycling helmet, a single key, a light switch on its plate and a round green handwash bottle.

Ask your child

"Where does the first-aid box live?" (say your real spot) "When does the helmet go on?" (before wheels) "Whose job is the key?" (the grown-ups’ — up high)

What your child can say or do

Your child might parade in the helmet all afternoon, restock the first-aid box like a nurse, or switch off every light in empty rooms with great authority.

Out in the real world

The same guardians stand watch in every home you visit — ask your hosts where the first-aid box lives. Knowing to ask is half the lesson already learned.

Try it together

Guardian Tour: draw the house as a simple map, and the child marks X on each guardian’s home — first-aid box, helmet, handwash sinks. The map goes on the fridge; safety has addresses now.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we put on before wheels?" (the helmet) "Where does the key stay?" (up high — grown-up treasure) "What do we do at the sink?" (handwash)

This lesson pairs with the Safe at Home flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Home Safety — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the machines and habits that guard the house — before any of them are ever needed, so the loud ones are already friends.

What is this?

The protectors: the smoke alarm with its loud voice, the torch (the flashlight) for dark corners, the safety gate on the stairs, the fire extinguisher and reflective vest for the grown-ups.

What does it mean?

A smoke alarm is a friend with a loud voice — said long before it ever beeps for real. Children who know the machines are startled by nothing and helped by all of it.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the real protectors: find the alarm (do not test the sound with a small child in the room), test the torch button, point at the gate.

Why this matters

The torch-flashlight pair lives right on the card, and the meeting-spot plan is the lesson’s quietly serious half: stop, go outside, meet at the tree — rehearsed as a game, known as a plan.

What it teaches

Emergency-machine familiarity (loud is warning, not danger), a family meeting plan, and the grown-up-tools category said warmly: grown-ups use, children know.

Words to learn

smoke alarmtorchflashlightsafety gatefire extinguisherreflective vest

Say this to your child

“"Home safety! The smoke alarm is a friend with a loud voice — if it beeps, we go outside and meet at the tree. The torch lights the dark. You know the plan."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "these five guard our house — let us meet them all."
  2. The smoke alarm: point at the real one — a friend with a loud voice. If it beeps, we go outside. That is its whole job.
  3. The torch: test the button in a dim corner — the child drives the beam. Flashlight, torch: both names, one light.
  4. The safety gate: find it, walk to it, say what it keeps little ones safe from.
  5. The plan, rehearsed once: if the alarm says beep-beep-beep — stop, go outside, meet at the tree. Then the extinguisher and vest: grown-up tools, child-known.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Home Safety" sit over a round ceiling smoke alarm, a blue torch, a stair safety gate, a red fire extinguisher and a hi-vis reflective vest.

Ask your child

"What does the smoke alarm say when it works?" (beep — loud — we go outside) "What lights the dark?" (the torch — the flashlight) "Where do we meet outside?" (say your real spot)

What your child can say or do

Your child might rehearse the meeting-spot march for fun, guard the torch like a lighthouse keeper, or explain the loud friend to every visitor.

Out in the real world

Hotels and grandparent houses have alarms and exits too — the child who knows the plan at home looks for the meeting spot everywhere. That habit is worth carrying.

Try it together

Meeting-Tree Drill: one sunny day, walk the plan as a game — from the bedroom, out the door, to the tree, everyone counted. Repeat any season, any mood. The drill is the comfort.

Staying safe

The extinguisher and the vest are grown-up tools — said with the words, every time. The alarm gets pointed at, never tested with small ears in the room, and the plan is rehearsed in daylight, calmly.

This lesson pairs with the Home Safety flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Water & Energy — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches where the house gets its power and its water — and turns saving both into a job with a badge, not a scolding.

What is this?

Water and energy: the tap that brings water, the light bulb that glows, the plug that feeds the machines, the water bottle that travels, the solar panel that catches sunshine.

What does it mean?

Children are magnificent absolutists — the tap is RUNNING! — and that exact energy is what saving runs on. The lesson aims it at two treasures and one proud day of patrolling.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the real utilities: a tap, a light switch, a plug (observed only). The solar panel may be on your roof, a neighbor’s, or only in books — all three count.

Why this matters

The plug rule is the safety spine of the card — plugs are grown-up hands — and it rides along with the fun instead of arriving as a lecture. The tap-faucet pair returns once more.

What it teaches

Resource awareness (where does it come from? where does it go?), habit-building (tap off while brushing), and the plug boundary said as fact.

Words to learn

tapfaucetlight bulbplugwater bottlesolar panelenergy

Say this to your child

“"Water and energy! The tap brings the drink, the bulb brings the light — and both are treasures. Tap off while brushing, lights off when we leave. You are the energy police today."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "our house drinks and glows — here is how."
  2. The tap: run it, count two seconds, off — and the brushing rule: tap off while teeth get brushed.
  3. The light bulb: switch one on, one off — lights for rooms we are IN.
  4. The plug: look with eyes only — the wall feeds the machines, and the wall side is a grown-up’s hands.
  5. The solar panel and the bottle: sunshine becomes power; the bottle refills again and again — the refillable habit.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Water and Energy" sit over a tap with one drop falling, a glowing light bulb, a two-pin plug, a labeled water bottle and a tilted solar panel.

Ask your child

"What brings the water?" (the tap — the faucet) "What should be off while we brush?" (the tap) "Whose hands touch the plug?" (the grown-up’s)

What your child can say or do

Your child might police every light in the postcode, time the tooth-brushing tap with real rigor, or ask whether the sun can charge the tablet.

Out in the real world

Utilities behave the same everywhere — hotels, holidays, school. The child who turns taps off at home does it in every bathroom they ever visit.

Try it together

Energy Police: one day on duty — a paper badge, a notebook of finds (light on in empty room! tap left running!) and one official report at dinner. Off duty tomorrow; the habits stay on.

Staying safe

Plugs and wall sockets are grown-up territory — eyes yes, hands no. Said as fact with the word, every time: the wall side belongs to grown-up hands.

This lesson pairs with the Water & Energy flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Recycling Words — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches recycling as a sorting sport: two bins, a stream of empties, and a child who learns that things do not end — they go around again.

What is this?

The recycling words: the glass bottle, the can, the cardboard box, the food scraps and the recycling bin — the materials and the home they go back to.

What does it mean?

Sorting is a two-year-old skill wearing a green badge. Name the materials — glass, metal, paper, food — and the child sorts forever, everywhere, with a referee’s joy.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, two labeled bins (recycling and rubbish) and a starter stream of clean empties. The compost corner can be real or imaginary — the food scraps need a home either way.

Why this matters

The compost is the wonder-word: food scraps become soil. Even explained simply, the loop — banana to soil to plant — is the deepest magic this set offers.

What it teaches

Material recognition (glass, metal, paper, food), sorting as a category skill, and the loop thinking that makes recycling feel like a fact of life rather than a rule.

Words to learn

glass bottlecancardboard boxfood scrapsrecycling bincompost

Say this to your child

“"Recycling words! The bottle, the can and the box go around again. The scraps feed the worms, the worms make the soil. Sorting game — on!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "things do not end — they go around. Here is how."
  2. Set the bins: recycling and rubbish, labeled by the child, placed side by side.
  3. Sort a starter stream together, naming materials: glass bottle — clink — recycling. Can — recycling. Cardboard — recycling. Banana peel — food scraps.
  4. The compost story, simply: the scraps go to the worms, the worms make soil, the soil grows more food.
  5. The child referees from now on — every empty gets dunked with ceremony.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Recycling Words" sit over a clear glass bottle, an unopened can, an open cardboard box, an apple core and banana peel, and a blue recycling bin with the loop arrows.

Ask your child

"Where does the glass bottle go?" (the recycling bin) "Where do the banana peels go?" (the food scraps — the compost) "What do the worms make?" (the soil)

What your child can say or do

Your child might interrogate every wrapper in the house, referee the grandparents’ sorting on visits, or guard the compost with quiet pride.

Out in the real world

Recycling runs in schools, parks and every town — bins with colors and rules. A child who sorts at home reads every public bin correctly, in any country.

Try it together

Bin Slam: hold up a clean empty — the child calls the material (glass! metal! paper! food!) and slam-dunks the right bin. Ten items, ten dunks, one very loud victory lap.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is the bottle made of?" (glass) "Where do the scraps go?" (the compost — the worms) "What do the arrows on the bin mean?" (it goes around again)

This lesson pairs with the Recycling Words flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Care for Earth — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson gathers the green ideas into one card — save energy, save water, recycle, reuse, care for Earth — and shrinks them to the only size that works: one job, one week, done daily.

What is this?

Care for Earth is the family of green habits: saving energy, saving water, recycling what we use, reusing what we can — all of it looking after the one planet everyone shares.

What does it mean?

One job done daily beats ten jobs done never. The lesson’s whole craft is the shrink: the whole Earth is too big for a four-year-old, but one light switch is exactly the right size.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, a paper badge and one chosen job for the week — the light-switch patrol, the tap-timer or the reuse-bag carrier.

Why this matters

Reuse is the newest word here: the bag used again, the jar refilled, the box turned into a garage. The idea lands fastest through the family’s own habits, caught rather than taught.

What it teaches

Habit formation (one job, one week, daily), cause-and-effect care (lights off means power saved), and planet-scale belonging — my home is inside a bigger home.

Words to learn

save energysave waterrecyclereusecare for Earthplanet

Say this to your child

“"Care for Earth — the biggest home of all! Lights off when we leave, tap off while we brush, bottles go around, bags get reused. Pick your job: the planet is hiring."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Earth is the biggest home there is — here is how we care for it."
  2. Read the five ideas with their gestures: lights off (fingers flick), tap off (wrist turn), recycle (loop), reuse (hug the bag), care for Earth (hands around the heart).
  3. Choose one Earth job for the week — the child chooses; the choosing is the buy-in.
  4. Make the badge: the job written on it, worn for the week, retired with honor.
  5. Friday review: what did we save? Numbers optional — pride mandatory.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Care for Earth" sit over a light bulb marked save energy, a tap marked save water, a recycling bin marked recycle, a refillable bottle marked reuse and a small tree marked care for Earth.

Ask your child

"What do we switch off when we leave a room?" (the light) "What gets reused?" (the bags — the jars — the boxes) "Whose job is the planet?" (everyone’s — starting with yours)

What your child can say or do

Your child might appoint themselves permanently to the light patrol, reuse every box into a toy garage, or comfort the tap personally each morning.

Out in the real world

Earth-care habits travel: park bins, school lights, the family car. A child with one green job at home notices every wasteful light in every building they enter — forever, useful.

Try it together

Earth Job Wheel: five jobs on a paper wheel — lights, tap, recycling, bags, plant-watering — spin it each Sunday. The wheel picks; the child performs; the planet quietly wins.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are the two treasures we save?" (water and energy) "What does reuse mean?" (use it again) "Who is the Earth job for this week?" (say the name proudly)

This lesson pairs with the Care for Earth flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Plants at Home — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the plant words through adoption: one real plant, one name, one small watering cup — and the whole vocabulary grows from there.

What is this?

The plants at home: the plant in its pot, the leaf that catches light, the flower that shows color, the tree that shades the yard, and the seed where every one of them began.

What does it mean?

A named plant is a watered plant — Ferdie the fern gets his cup twice as faithfully as an unnamed one. Ownership, not instruction, is what makes the habit grow.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, one houseplant (any survivor will do), a small cup for watering and a name, chosen with ceremony. The windowsill bean jar is the bonus experiment.

Why this matters

The seed is the hinge word: something fingernail-small becomes a tree. One bean in a jar on the windowsill proves it in two weeks — the set’s most reliable miracle.

What it teaches

Care routines for living things, observation over time (new leaf? new flower?), and the plant-body map — roots below, stem up, leaves out.

Words to learn

plantleafflowertreeseedpotgrow

Say this to your child

“"Plants at home! The leaf catches the light, the flower shows its colors — and every one of them started as a seed. Your plant has a name now; the cup is yours."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "our home has green residents — here are their words."
  2. Meet the parts on the card: the leaf catches the light, the flower shows its colors, the tree shades the yard.
  3. The seed story: every plant on this card started as a seed the size of a fingernail.
  4. The adoption: choose the plant, choose the name, hand over the watering cup — once a week, small drink.
  5. The bean jar to finish: bean, wet cotton, windowsill — and the watching begins.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Plants at Home" sit over a potted plant with wide leaves, a single green leaf, a white flower with a blue center, a round-crowned tree and one teardrop seed.

Ask your child

"What catches the light for the plant?" (the leaf) "What was every plant first?" (a seed) "Whose job is the watering cup?" (say the name — the adopter’s)

What your child can say or do

Your child might greet the plant by name each morning, measure the bean jar hourly, or assign leaves to the whole family as badges.

Out in the real world

Plants wait in every grandma’s window, every classroom, every park. A child who knows plant words and plant care is welcomed as a helper in all of them.

Try it together

Plant Diary: one page per week — the child draws their plant exactly as it is today. New leaf? New pot? The diary catches it all, and the habit of looking closely grows with the plant.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does every plant begin?" (a seed) "What part shows the colors?" (the flower) "Who waters Ferdie?" (the child — once a week, small cup)

This lesson pairs with the Plants at Home flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.

HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Caring for Plants — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the five things every plant needs — pot, soil, seed, water, sun — by planting one real seed that belongs entirely to the child.

What is this?

Caring for plants means giving them what they need: the pot to live in, the soil to root in, the seed to start from, the watering can to drink from, the sunlight to eat.

What does it mean?

A planted seed is a responsibility with a heartbeat — slow, forgiving, and entirely dependent on the child showing up. Miss a day, water twice; the plant forgives, and the habit forms.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, one small pot, seed compost, one big seed (a bean or sunflower — both forgiving), a small watering can and the brightest windowsill in the house.

Why this matters

The crayon-line height chart is the lesson’s celebration: when the sprout appears, its height is marked and dated. Growing things get measured; pride gets recorded.

What it teaches

Sequencing a living process (pot, soil, seed, water, sun), daily care with real stakes, and patience — the slowest virtue, taught by the fastest forgiving teacher.

Words to learn

plant potseedsoilwatering cansunlightsprout

Say this to your child

“"Caring for plants! Soil in the pot, seed tucked in, one small drink, the sunniest window. Now the best part — every morning, we look. One day soon: a sprout, and it is YOURS."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "five things every plant needs — we have all five."
  2. Pot first: the child names it (their pot, their choice) and fills it with soil — hands in the dirt, that is the lesson signing on.
  3. The seed: one big seed, one finger-deep hole, tucked in with a pat.
  4. Water and sun: one small glug from the can — then the brightest sill, and the promise: we check every day.
  5. The waiting, done right: one check each morning, a small drink when the soil is dry — and when the sprout comes, the crayon line and the date.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Caring for Plants" sit over a terracotta plant pot, one fat seed, a mound of dark soil, a blue watering can mid-pour and a bright sun with rays.

Ask your child

"What does the seed tuck into?" (the soil) "What does the plant drink?" (water from the can) "What does the plant eat?" (the sunlight)

What your child can say or do

Your child might check the pot before breakfast in pajamas, water it with tea-party precision, or draw the sprout taller than it is — with artistic license and total joy.

Out in the real world

Gardens, classrooms and community plots all run this sequence — pot, soil, seed, water, sun. A child who has raised one sprout is a gardener wherever a pot is offered.

Try it together

Sprout Height Chart: when the sprout appears, mark its height with a crayon line and the date — then mark again each week. The chart becomes the family’s slowest, proudest graph.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are the five things a plant needs?" (pot, soil, seed, water, sun) "How often do we check?" (every morning) "Whose sprout is it?" (say the name — the grower’s)

This lesson pairs with the Caring for Plants flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.
